title: The Paper Trail Before an Agent Writes Code
description: Nine tools that make an agent show its work: specs, maps, approvals, detection rules, exposure audits, runners and deployment journals.
tldr: Spec-First writes a reviewed spec before any code exists, Trama keeps a map of your app that every agent change has to pass through as a Proposal, and hackerscad makes the CAD model itself reviewable code. FENGARDE is a 46-rule OCSF detection pipeline, Dante audits what a coding agent can reach on your machine, Virgil routes tasks through a local library before calling a model, Sectr journals every message and approval, MCPTask runs autonomous developers against a public backlog, and Marlow hands you the generated source.
content:
# The Paper Trail Before an Agent Writes Code

The first generation of coding agents optimised for one thing: getting from a prompt to a diff as fast as possible. The tools below are the reaction to that. Each one inserts a record, a spec, a map, a rule, an approval, a journal, between what you asked for and what lands in your repository.

## Describe it, then review the description

[[link:/tools/2195|Spec-First]] inverts the usual order. You describe a feature in your own words, and create-spec writes goal, facts with file and line references, steps and done criteria onto a fresh branch in its own worktree. No code yet. A script then checks that every cited file and line actually exists, and a second agent with no chat history attacks the spec against the code, with its cuts applied before anything is built. Only then does apply-spec work through the steps and write the tests the spec named, logging every non-obvious choice, and deliver-spec runs your checks. Specs are plain YAML and Markdown in your repository, it is MIT licensed, and it runs as a Claude Code plugin or with any agent.

## The map, and what happens when it disagrees

[[link:/tools/2196|Trama]] keeps a map of your app next to the code as plain Markdown in a .trama directory, drawn as a diagram. The agent reads the map before it writes a line, and every change arrives as a Proposal you approve before any code exists. You describe the change, answer only the questions the agent cannot resolve from memory or the repository, approve, then run the tasks. The clever part is the Drift: when the code and the map stop telling the same story, Trama raises it and you decide which one is right. It supports VS Code 1.106 or later only.

## The model is code, so it can be reviewed

[[link:/tools/2189|hackerscad]] applies the same principle to geometry. It is parametric CAD where the model is code, written in a small sandboxed language with units, selectors and libraries, and the 3D view follows as you type. Every mouse edit is written back into the file, so fillets, holes and patterns land as readable code rather than an opaque binary. Parts are checked with unittest blocks, and the command line checks, renders and exports in CI. It also ships an MCP server and a skill file, so an agent can install itself, read the language from docs written for agents, and render what it built.

## Forty-six rules you can read

[[link:/tools/2188|FENGARDE]] is an open-source, self-hosted security pipeline for IT, AI and OT that turns a raw log line into a verified incident and a draft NIS2 notification. It normalises to OCSF, ships 46 detection rules tagged against MITRE ATT&CK, ATLAS and ICS, and runs nine services over one bus, so no service calls another and any stage can be restarted or swapped alone. A capability board states honestly what is on time, on request, a replacement or cancelled, and a replay button runs a recorded lab attack or a generated AI-to-OT chain through the real console. Apache-2.0.

## What the agent can reach on your machine

The threat model that signature antivirus was built for assumes something malicious gets installed. [[link:/tools/2187|Dante AI Agent Antivirus]] starts from a different one: a coding agent runs with your rights and needs to install nothing at all to read your .env file, your SSH keys and your shell history. Dante checks the places an agent or a thief reaches for, leaked keys, SSH, MCP configs, servers, and shows the proof line behind every verdict. It runs offline with no account, ships as MIT-licensed plain JavaScript with no dependencies and no install scripts, and extends through signed data packs that carry rules rather than code. It reports exposure rather than blocking it, which is the honest scope for a tool you can read end to end.

## Check the library before you spend the call

[[link:/tools/2206|Virgil CLI]] attacks the cost side of the same problem from a different angle. It keeps four local libraries, speech, debug, code and UI/HTML, and on every task checks them against your request first. A match answers with no model call. A partial pattern adapts with one call. Only when it has nothing does it solve from scratch, and it stores the result for next time. Injection runs through your own APIs, your own server, or the central backbone it ships with. The libraries start empty, which means the tool is worth exactly as much as the repetition in your week.

## One source of truth for every message and approval

[[link:/tools/2198|Sectr]] is a serverless backend for deploying agents, and the thing it sells is the journal. You keep writing agents in LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK or Pydantic AI, add two lines, and stream to any frontend over AG-UI. No restructuring into workflows, and no checkpointer, because the Sectr journal is the checkpoint. Mark a tool as needing approval and the agent scales to zero while it waits for a human, with the request recorded. Free during beta.

## Watch it until merge

[[link:/tools/2200|MCPTask]] runs autonomous AI developers against a real backlog and publishes the whole path: task, branch, pull request, tests and merge. Its runners work around the clock on its own machines and none of them has direct access to the main branch. A live page shows the open-source mcp4mail project being built, with 182 finished tasks delivered in 42 days, and the site is redeployed once a day so you can confirm that what merged is what shipped. If you want to know whether an autonomous developer is trustworthy, watching one work on someone else's repository for six weeks is a reasonable way to find out.

## You keep the code

[[link:/tools/2208|Marlow]] takes the position that the output of an AI builder should be yours: it turns ideas into real applications with AI, and you keep the code, the infrastructure and the freedom to deploy anywhere. It is in beta and the public pages are thin, but the ownership claim is the one that matters, because the alternative is a codebase that only exists inside somebody else's product.

## The shape of the next phase

Every tool here is a bet that the bottleneck has moved. Generating the code stopped being the hard part; knowing what was generated, why, and whether it was allowed is now the hard part. Specs, maps, rules, approvals, journals and ownership are all the same bet wearing different clothes, and the fact that nine of them turned up in one week suggests the bet is being placed widely.
